title: BBR Button Board
text: BBR Button Board A button box you build out of tiles. One USB cable to the Driver Station. The Button Board is a modular control panel for FIRST robotics. A main module plugs into the Driver Station laptop over USB and presents itself as a game controller. Everything a driver actually touches lives on tiles — nine-key keypads, single keys, arcade buttons, rotary encoders — daisy-chained off the main module on one four-wire cable. Build the panel you want. Tiles chain in any order. No code on the robot. The board is an ordinary game controller. Your OpMode or robot code reads buttons exactly the way it reads a gamepad. Works with both Driver Stations. An FRC-friendly HID gamepad with 32 buttons, or an XInput gamepad for the FTC Driver Station — one setting, no hardware change. Configured in the browser. Bind a key by pressing it. No firmware rebuild, no config file. Keys that relabel themselves. A screen key has a colour display inside the cap, so one key can say INTAKE in one part of a match and CLIMB in another. A colour display tile shows the same kind of pictures beside the keys. LEDs your robot drives. Keys on RGB tiles change colour with what the robot is doing. In FTC the OpMode does it directly: bind a rumble code to key colours in the config app, and one rumble() call recolours them, and switches a screen key’s legend at the same time. In FRC a companion app on the Driver Station laptop drives them. How it fits together Driver Station laptop │ USB-C ┌────┴──────┐ RS-485, one cable per link │ main ├──── tile ──── tile ──── tile │ module │ └───────────┘ The main module polls every tile in turn, collects which keys are down, and sends one USB report. From the Driver Station’s point of view there is a single game controller with 32 buttons on it. Start here If you want to Read Know what the parts are What you have Put a panel together Plugging it together Get buttons working First run Decide which key does what Binding buttons Light the panel from robot state Driver Station app Change a legend or picture mid-match Display tiles and legends The board is not a keyboard and does not run your robot code. Nothing on the robot has to change to use one. The exception is changing a screen key’s legend during a match, which needs a few lines in your OpMode — see Changing legends in a match.

title: What you have
text: What you have The main module One per panel. It has the USB-C socket, the processor that runs the bus, and two tile connectors. Connects to Driver Station laptop, USB-C Presents itself as A game controller — 32 buttons, 4 axes Drives Up to 31 tiles on one chain Also carries The CFG button The main module holds the whole configuration: which key is which button, what colour each LED is, and which USB personality to use. Tiles hold none of it, so a tile can be swapped for an identical one without reconfiguring anything. The tiles Every tile has a small processor, a transceiver and two connectors. They differ in their keys, encoders or display. Tile What it is Keys Grid mx1 / mx1rgb A single Cherry MX hot-swap key 1 2 × 1 mx1 1x1 / mx1rgb 1x1 The same key on the smallest board, cables out the back 1 1 × 1 mx3 / mx3rgb Three keys in a row 3 3 × 1 mx4 / mx4rgb Four keys as a WASD cluster 4 3 × 2 mx6rgb Six keys in a 3 × 2 grid, an RGB LED under each 6 3 × 3 arc4 Four arcade buttons, each on a 3-pin JST PH lead 4 2 × 1 enc1 One rotary encoder with a push-to-click shaft 1 encoder + 1 key 2 × 1 enc2 Two rotary encoders with push-to-click shafts 2 encoders + 2 keys 2 × 2 disp1 A 128 × 32 text panel — a readout, not a control none 2 × 1 disp2 A 160 × 128 colour display: text, and stored pictures none 2 × 2 screenkey1 One key whose cap is a 128 × 128 colour screen 1 2 × 1 The rgb versions are the same board with a colour LED under every key. See LED colours. The splitter, a small board with no processor, has four connectors so the chain can branch. Every tile, with pictures and what each can do, is on The tiles. disp1, disp2 and screenkey1 are the display tiles. On screenkey1 the screen is the key’s legend. See Display tiles and legends. Keys on a tile are numbered from 0. Buttons the Driver Station sees are numbered from 1. See Binding buttons. Hot-swap means the key switches push in and pull out by hand, with no soldering. What you supply A USB-C cable to the Driver Station laptop. That is the only power the panel needs. Tile cables — one per link in the chain, six-way JST GH, straight through. Key switches and keycaps for the MX tiles, or arcade buttons for arc4. Any Cherry MX-compatible switch fits. Cases, if you want them: 3D-printed, for an openGrid board. See Printing the cases. What the Driver Station sees Personality Driver Station You get frc FRC (Windows) 32 buttons and 4 axes on one HID gamepad xinput FTC (Driver Hub / phone) An Xbox-360-style gamepad; the 32 buttons map onto its controls Change it in the config app, unplug, plug back in. See The config app.

title: The tiles
text: The tiles Every tile is its own small board on the bus, with two identical cable connectors, so tiles can be mixed in any combination and any order (see Plugging it together). This page describes what each one is and what you can do with it. Most tiles come in a plain version and an RGB version. The RGB version is the same board with a colour LED under every key. It reports the same tile type, plus its LEDs, so anything that works on the plain tile works on the RGB one. The LEDs add colours, a white flash when a key is pressed, and colours the robot can change during a match. See LED colours. Sizes are the bare board. Grid is the case’s size in 28 mm openGrid cells; see Printing the cases. Key tiles All key tiles take Cherry MX-compatible switches in hot-swap sockets: the switches push in by hand, with no soldering. Each key can be bound to any of the 32 buttons, several keys can share one button, and one key can press several buttons at once. See Binding buttons. mx1 and mx1rgb One key, centred on the board. Keys 1 LEDs mx1rgb: 1 Size 40 × 20 mm Grid 2 × 1 mx1 1x1 and mx1rgb 1x1 The same single key on the smallest board, for a 1 × 1 cell. Both cable connectors are on the back, side by side, so both cables leave from the back along one edge. Keys 1 LEDs mx1rgb 1x1: 1 Size 25 × 25 mm Grid 1 × 1 mx3 and mx3rgb Three keys in a row. The RGB version is 2 mm taller, so the two do not share a case; only mx3rgb has one so far. Keys 3 LEDs mx3rgb: 3 Size mx3: 66 × 20 mm; mx3rgb: 66 × 22 mm Grid mx3rgb: 3 × 1 mx4 and mx4rgb Four keys as a WASD cluster: three in a row with one above the middle. Key 1 is the top key (W), and keys 2 to 4 are the bottom row from left to right (A, S, D). Keys 4 LEDs mx4rgb: 4 Size 57 × 39 mm Grid 3 × 2 mx6rgb Six keys in a 3 × 2 grid, each with a colour LED. Six LEDs at full white still fit the default USB power budget. Keys 6 LEDs 6 Size 60 × 60 mm Grid 3 × 3 Arcade buttons arc4 Four arcade buttons, each on its own 3-pin JST PH lead. The buttons are panel-mounted wherever you want them, and the tile sits behind the panel. The leads carry ground, the button’s switch, and +5 V for a lamp in the button. The lamp feed is always on; the board does not switch it. Buttons 4 Size 50 × 25 mm Grid 2 × 1 Rotary encoders An encoder is a knob that turns without an end stop and clicks as it turns. Each one also presses in, like a key. A turn can drive an axis, press a button once per click, or, on an FTC Driver Station, count on a trigger so the robot code can read the knob’s position. See Rotary encoders. enc1 One encoder, centred. Encoders 1, with push Size 44 × 20 mm Grid 2 × 1 enc2 Two encoders side by side. Encoders 2, each with push Size 50 × 50 mm Grid 2 × 2 Display tiles Display tiles show text, and the colour ones also show pictures. You can write to them from the config app, and the robot can change what they show during a match by sending a number, a legend code. See Display tiles and legends and Changing legends in a match. disp1 A 0.91” 128 × 32 monochrome text panel. A readout, not a control: it has no keys. The robot can swap its text between prewritten messages. Display 128 × 32 mono, 21 characters × 4 rows Size 50 × 20 mm Grid 2 × 1 disp2 A 1.8” colour display, 160 × 128, landscape. It shows coloured text, and it stores up to 32 pictures on the tile, so the robot can switch between them instantly. Display 160 × 128 colour, 13 characters × 8 rows Pictures 32 stored Size 50 × 40 mm Grid 2 × 2 screenkey1 One key whose keycap is a 128 × 128 colour screen, so the key’s label can change: INTAKE while collecting, CLIMB in the endgame. The screen key module stands on the case and plugs into the tile on a short cable. Like disp2, it stores up to 32 pictures. Keys 1 Display 128 × 128 colour, 10 characters × 8 rows Pictures 32 stored Size 50 × 22 mm Grid 2 × 1, or 2 × 2 to hide the cable Bus parts This has no processor and does not show up as a tile. It only shapes the cabling. Splitter Four connectors wired together, one on each edge, so the chain can branch. See Splitting the chain. Connectors 4 Size 20 × 20 mm Grid 1 × 1

title: Printing the cases
text: Printing the cases Every board has a 3D-printed case that snaps into an openGrid board, lite or full. A case takes a whole number of 28 mm grid cells, and every case stands 15 mm tall, so a panel of tiles reads as one flat surface. Each case is a base, which snaps into the grid, and a lid, which snaps into the base and finishes flush with its walls. Downloads Each zip has the parts as STEP, for editing in Fusion or any CAD program, and as STL, ready to slice. It also has the case’s README, with what it fits and how it goes together. Case Fits Grid Download Main module the main module 2 × 1 case-main-module.zip Splitter the bus splitter 1 × 1 case-splitter.zip mx1 1x1 the 25 mm single key, mx1-1x1 and mx1rgb-1x1 1 × 1 case-mx1-1x1.zip mx1 the single key, mx1 and mx1rgb 2 × 1 case-mx1rgb.zip mx3rgb three keys in a row, mx3rgb 3 × 1 case-mx3rgb.zip mx4 the WASD cluster, mx4 and mx4rgb 3 × 2 case-mx4.zip mx6rgb six keys in a 3 × 2 grid, mx6rgb 3 × 3 case-mx6rgb.zip arc4 four arcade buttons 2 × 1 case-arc4.zip enc1 one rotary encoder 2 × 1 case-enc1.zip enc2 two rotary encoders 2 × 2 case-enc2.zip disp1 the 128 × 32 text panel 2 × 1 case-disp1.zip disp2 the 1.8” colour display 2 × 2 case-disp2.zip screenkey1 the screen key; its cable shows on the north side 2 × 1 case-screenkey1.zip screenkey1, cable bay the screen key with its cable hidden in an 8 mm bay 2 × 1, overhangs north case-screenkey1-bay.zip screenkey1, 2x2 the screen key with its cable hidden, nothing overhanging 2 × 2 case-screenkey1-2x2.zip Cable tiles no board: fill an empty cell, or carry tile cables across it. Blank, straight, corner, tee, cross, and drop, which takes a cable up through the grid from behind 1 × 1 case-cable-1x1.zip Low cable tiles the back of the board: thin, 3.75 mm tall, so cables run behind the panel. Straight, corner, tee, cross, and drop. Every one has a hole at its centre, so a cable can come through the board at any of them. Needs a full (double-sided) openGrid board 1 × 1 case-cable-1x1-low.zip Back plate the back of the board: a cover that holds the cables flat, on snap-in supports. This zip is the 5 × 5 plate; make one for your board’s size. Needs a full (double-sided) openGrid board your board case-back-plate.zip The screen key cases also have a hood, a third part that holds the screen module down on the lid. Printing Base: print it the way it sits, with the snap on the bed. Lid: print it top-down. The STL is already flipped. The latch tabs then point up and need no supports. No part needs supports. For the key tiles, the lid is also the switch plate, with 14.0 mm square holes. If switches are loose or tight in your print, the case README says which setting to change. Putting a case together Drop the board into the base. Press the lid in until its latches click. It sits flush with the walls. For the key tiles, push the switches through the lid into the hot-swap sockets. Snap the base into the openGrid board. To open a case, pull the switches first, if it has any. Then lift the lid at the small notch in its rim with a fingernail or a small screwdriver.

title: Back plate for the leads
text: Back plate for the leads Leads that drop through the openGrid board hang loose behind the panel. The back plate holds them flat: a plate the size of your board, standing a few millimetres off its back, held by snap-in supports. The plate has a hole on every cell, so a support can go in any free cell, around the cells your drop tiles already use. Each support snaps into the back of the board like a low cable tile, and its post clips up through the plate’s hole. The post is hollow, 10.4 mm across. A lead can still come through the board at a support’s cell, so placing a support never costs you a drop position. You need a full openGrid board. The supports snap into the back of the board, as the low cable tiles do. A lite board is single-sided and has nothing to snap into. Make your plate Set the size of your board in cells, then download the two parts. The page builds the plate for that size. You print one plate and several supports from the support STL. The generator needs JavaScript. Without it, the 5 × 5 plate and its supports are in case-back-plate.zip. Gap is the space between the back of the board and the plate. At the default 5 mm, twisted leads, a plug lying flat, and the 3.75 mm low cable tiles all fit under it. A bigger gap leaves more room, and the clip gets easier to push in. Plate hole is for your printer. Make it a little bigger if the clips won’t go through, or a little smaller if the plate rattles. Printing Plate: flat on the bed. Supports: the way they sit, with the snap on the bed. They need no supports. The clip has to flex as it goes through the plate. At the 5 mm gap that is near the limit of PLA. If PLA clips crack, print the supports in PETG. Fitting it Snap the supports into the back of the board: one near each corner, and more across the middle on a big board. The generator suggests how many. Route your leads across the back. A lead can come through any free cell, or up through a support’s post. Lay the plate over the posts and press down over each one until it clicks. To take the plate off, squeeze the clip at the top of each post and lift that corner.

title: Plugging it together
text: Plugging it together The chain Every board — the main module and every tile — has two identical connectors, wired in parallel. Run a cable from one board to the next in any order you like: Each arrow is one cable. The arrows only show the order the boards were cabled in; the bus itself runs both ways. Order does not matter. Both connectors on a board are the same. There is no “in” and no “out”. Cables are straight through. Pin 1 to pin 1. There is no crossover cable in this system. Up to 31 tiles, and up to about 4 m of cable in total. Splitting the chain A splitter is a small square board with four connectors wired in parallel. Use one where the cable wants to go in more than one direction, for example along both sides of a panel: Tiles on a branch work exactly like tiles on the main run. No loops. Never cable back to a board that is already on the bus. Nothing detects a loop. Count the branches in the 4 m. The limit is the total of every cable on the bus. Power The whole panel runs off the USB cable. There is nothing else to plug in. The main module turns the global LED brightness down until the worst-case draw of the chain fits the USB power budget, so a panel with many LEDs runs dimmer. If you are running from a port that can supply more than the default, raise the budget in the config app. See LED colours. Adding a tile mid-season Plug it into a spare connector. The main module gives it an address by itself the next time it is powered on. Nothing that was already bound changes. Bindings are stored per tile position, not per physical board. If you swap a faulty tile for an identical one, the replacement inherits the old one’s bindings automatically. If you add a second tile of the same kind, it is a new tile and starts unbound. Binding buttons covers what to do when the board cannot tell which case it is looking at. Cable pinout Six-way JST GH, 1.25 mm pitch. You only need this if you are making cables. Pin Signal 1 GND 2 GND 3 B (−) 4 A (+) 5 5 V 6 5 V

title: First run
headings: 3. Check the board sees your tiles
6. Point the Driver Station at it
text: First run Plug in, bind a key, check it registers. 1. Plug it in Connect the tiles into a chain and plug the main module into your laptop with a USB-C cable. The power LED comes on immediately. The laptop should find a new game controller by itself — no driver, no install. On Windows, joy.cpl (Start → Run → joy.cpl) shows it. 2. Open the config app Go to https://configure.buttonboard.buildingblockrobotics.com in Chrome or Edge and press Connect. The browser shows a list of serial ports; pick the Button Board. Chrome or Edge only. Firefox and Safari do not support Web Serial, which the config app needs. The page tells you if your browser is not supported. The Connect screen then shows what the board is: firmware version, serial number, how many tiles it can see, and which USB personality is active. 3. Check the board sees your tiles Switch to Diagnose. Every tile in the chain should be listed as online, with the tile kind and how many keys it has. If a tile is missing, work through Troubleshooting. Check first for a cable not clicked fully home. Press keys. Diagnose shows presses live, before any binding, so you can check each switch works. 4. Bind a key Go to Configure. The chain is down the left; pick a tile and it is drawn the way it physically is, keys in the right places. Click the key you want to bind. In the inspector, choose the logical button it should be — 1 to 32. Press the key. The board confirms it. Repeat for as many keys as you need. Unbound buttons never press. 5. Save Press Save. Until you do, the configuration lives in RAM and is lost on the next power cycle. Saved configuration survives unplugging, reboots and firmware updates of the tiles. 6. Point the Driver Station at it FRC: the board appears as a 32-button joystick. Assign it a port in the Driver Station the way you would any joystick. FTC: switch the USB personality to xinput on the Connect screen, then unplug and plug back in. The personality only changes when the board is replugged. The Driver Hub then sees an Xbox-style gamepad, and Start+A / Start+B binds it as gamepad 1 or 2 as usual. Nothing works and nothing shows up? Hold the CFG button on the main module while you plug the USB cable in. That forces a known-good configuration personality, whatever is stored. Testing without a robot The Diagnose screen can make the board report button presses that no one is touching — one button at a time walking 1 → 32, one button held, or all of them at once. Use it to check the Driver Station end works before any tile is bound. Test mode ends when you disconnect.

title: Updating the firmware
text: Updating the firmware Tiles and the main module update in different ways. Both start from the Firmware screen of the config app. Tiles Tiles update over the bus. Nothing is unplugged and no programmer is needed. One tile updates at a time; the rest of the chain keeps working. Open Firmware in the config app. Any tile running older firmware than the images the site carries is listed with an Update button. Press it and wait. Progress is shown as it goes. The tile drops out of the chain for a few seconds and rejoins when it is done. Its address and its bindings are untouched. A tile that loses power partway through an update is not bricked. It comes back on its old firmware. The main module The main module updates over USB by drag-and-drop. Press Update main module in the config app. The board reboots into its bootloader, and the COM port disappears. This is expected; the config app reports the lost connection. A USB drive called RPI-RP2 appears on your computer. Drag the .uf2 file onto it. The drive disappears and the board restarts on the new firmware. Your configuration — bindings, LED colours, USB personality — survives the update. If the config app cannot reach the board at all, unplug the board, hold the BOOTSEL button, plug it back in, and release. RPI-RP2 appears the same way. Which versions am I on? The Connect screen reports the main module’s firmware version, and Diagnose reports each tile’s. Mixed versions across tiles are fine. Diagnose flags any tile whose protocol is not compatible.

title: The config app
text: The config app Everything is configured in a browser at https://configure.buttonboard.buildingblockrobotics.com, with nothing to install. The page talks to the board directly over USB; your configuration never leaves the laptop. Chrome or Edge, on a desktop. The app uses Web Serial, which Firefox, Safari and mobile browsers do not support. Press Connect and pick the board from the browser’s port list. The first time, the board has to be selected by hand. Five screens Connect Board identity: product, firmware version, serial number, tile count, and whether the stored configuration is valid. This is also where the USB personality is set — frc for the FRC Driver Station, xinput for FTC. The change is stored immediately but only takes effect on the next USB reset, so unplug and plug back in after switching. Configure The panel as it physically is. The chain runs down the left; select a tile and it is drawn in its real layout, so you can click the key itself. Selecting a key opens the inspector, which does three things: binds it to a logical button, adds it to a group with other keys, and sets its LED colour. See Binding buttons and LED colours. Select a display tile and the inspector offers what that tile can do instead: text and a bar on the panel, Messages saved under legend codes, a Picture to send or store, the tile’s Slots, and the Legend codes that let robot code switch between them. See Display tiles and legends. Legends Every legend code, 1 to 15, and what it does across the whole board: the picture it shows, the messages it writes and the key colours it sets, with the call the robot sends for it. Edit opens the tile that holds an entry. See Seeing every code at once. Diagnose The state of the bus. Tiles — every tile the board knows about, its kind, its firmware, whether it is online, and which keys are down right now. Counters — checksum errors and missed replies per tile. Both should sit at zero; a tile that is steadily accumulating either has a cable problem. Power — the LED power budget, the worst-case draw of the current panel, and the brightness that fits it. Test — makes the board report button presses with no tile involved, for checking the Driver Station end on its own. Firmware Updates for the tiles over the bus, and for the main module over USB. See Updating the firmware. Saved versus not saved Changes take effect immediately — bind a key and it works on the next press — but they live in RAM until you press Save. The app shows when there are unsaved changes. A power cycle discards unsaved changes and returns the board to its last saved configuration. Without a board The config app runs against a built-in fake board with a few tiles on it, so the interface can be used with nothing plugged in.

title: Binding buttons
headings: What happens when a tile disappears
text: Binding buttons Keys and buttons A key is a physical thing on a tile. Keys are numbered from 0 within their tile, and a key on its own does nothing. A logical button is what the Driver Station sees. There are 32 of them, numbered 1 to 32, and they exist whether or not anything is bound to them. Binding connects the two. Until a key is bound, pressing it registers nowhere. Robot code refers to the button number, so it does not change when Button 7 moves to a different key, tile, or kind of tile. Binding a key In Configure, click the key on its tile. The Reports as panel shows the 32 buttons twice: as a numbered grid, and placed on an Xbox-style gamepad. Click a button in either view to bind the key to it. The bound button is highlighted. Under each number is the Xbox control that button becomes in FTC (xinput) mode. Buttons 25–32 have no Xbox control, so FTC mode does not send them. To bind by pressing instead, click Press a key… and press the key on the board. It takes the button shown, or the next free one if the selected key is not bound. Rebinding a key to a different button replaces the old binding, including any combo the key was part of. Groups: several keys, one button Several keys can feed the same button. The button is pressed while any of them is down. Use this for: The same action reachable from two ends of a wide panel. A driver and a co-driver who each need the same override. An arcade button and a keypad key that do the same job. Add the key to an existing button rather than replacing it. Up to 16 keys can share one button. Combos: one key, several buttons One key can press several buttons at once, and releasing it releases them all together. This is for FTC: the Driver Station assigns a pad to gamepad 1 when it sees Start+A, and to gamepad 2 on Start+B. Bind each combo to one key. In Configure, click the key, then: Start+A or Start+B sets that combo in one click. Combo turns on toggling: each number you click is added to the key, or taken off it. Click Combo again to go back to picking one button. The key shows every button it feeds, for example B1+8. A combo does not take the buttons away from other keys: a key bound to Start+A and a separate key bound to Start both work. If the buttons in a combo have different LED colours, the key shows the colour of the lowest-numbered one. The Driver Station sees every button in a combo change in the same instant, not Start first and then A. Whether the Driver Hub accepts simultaneous presses has not been tested on one yet. If it does not, bind Start and A to two separate keys. Debounce The tile debounces every key. The default is 5 ms, or 20 ms on arc4. To change it, select the tile in Configure and set Debounce, under the tile, from 1 to 255 ms. It applies to every key on that tile, and every press on that tile is delayed by the same amount. Default puts it back. Press Save to keep it. Raise it if a switch chatters, usually a worn arcade microswitch. What happens when a tile disappears If a tile stops answering — cable pulled, board damaged — every button bound to it reads as released, immediately. Bindings to a missing tile are kept, not deleted, so a tile that is unplugged and plugged back in keeps its bindings. Swapping and replacing tiles Bindings are stored against a tile’s position on the bus, and the board remembers which physical tile was in each position. Replace a broken tile with an identical one — the new tile takes the old one’s place and its bindings, automatically. Add another tile of the same kind — it is a new tile, and starts unbound. When the board cannot tell those two cases apart, it says so, and the config app offers the choice. Saving Bindings work as soon as they are made, but live in RAM until you press Save. Save writes them to flash and reads them back to check.

title: LED colours
headings: Colours follow the button, not the key
A key with no button as an indicator light
text: LED colours Tiles with RGB keys — the ones whose name ends in rgb, such as mx4rgb and mx6rgb — have one addressable LED under every key. There are two independent ways to drive them. Two layers Defaults are part of your saved configuration. They are what the panel looks like when it powers up: a red key for the emergency stop, blue for the intake, dark for everything unbound. Set them in the config app’s Configure screen, and press Save. The live layer is set at runtime, over USB, by a companion app on the Driver Station laptop. It is never saved. Use it to, for example, flash the arm button red while the arm is out of bounds, or light the scoring buttons only when the robot is in range. In FTC mode there is no USB channel for a companion app, but the robot can still write the live layer: a rumble code can be set up to recolour keys. See Changing a key’s colour the same way. The live layer wins wherever both are set, per LED. Clearing it returns every LED to the saved defaults. See Driver Station app for how to write to it. Colours follow the button, not the key An LED colour set for a logical button moves with that button. Rebind Button 7 to a different key and its colour goes with it. LEDs that are not under a bound key — edge glow, spare positions — are addressed by tile and LED number instead. A key with no button as an indicator light A key does not have to press anything to have a colour. Select a key that is not bound in Configure, and its LED section gives the key a colour of its own. It stays lit whether or not the key has a keycap, so you can pull the keycap and use that position as an indicator light. The robot can change it during a match too. The same key’s Robot colour section works as it does for a bound key. See Changing a key’s colour the same way. If you later bind the key to a button that has a colour, the button’s colour takes over. Unbind it again and the key’s own colour comes back. Effects Effect What it does solid On, steady. The default. blink Slow flash fast Fast flash breathe Smooth fade in and out Once set, an effect keeps running without a companion app sending anything further. Press feedback By default a key flashes white while it is held, over whatever colour it was showing. Where several keys share a button, this shows which one was pressed. You can change the feedback colour, or turn it off per button. A key whose button has no colour does not flash by default: there is no LED setting for it at all. To get the flash without a colour, select the key in Configure and turn on Flash when pressed in its LED section. The key then stays dark and lights white only while it is held. The same switch turns the flash off on a key that has a colour. Brightness and the power budget The whole panel runs off the USB cable, and the LEDs draw most of that power. The main module adds up the worst-case draw of every tile on the chain and lowers the global brightness until the total fits the budget. Adding another lit tile dims the whole panel slightly. The Diagnose → Power view shows all three numbers: the budget, the worst case, and the brightness actually in use. If you are running from a port that can supply more than the default, raise the budget there. If a panel cannot fit even at minimum brightness, the board holds the LEDs off and raises a fault. The Power view says so. Turning everything off There is a single “all LEDs off” command, and it takes priority over anything else in flight. Use it when a panel is doing something unexpected on a field.

title: Rotary encoders
text: Rotary encoders The enc2 tile carries two rotary encoders, each with a push-to-click shaft. Use them for continuous values — arm setpoint, shooter speed, LED brightness on the robot. What the Driver Station sees FRC. Each encoder can be bound to one of four axes. The axis reports an accumulated position — turn it clockwise and the number goes up, keep turning and it keeps going. There are four axes in total, so two enc2 tiles claim all of them. An axis does not spring back to centre and has no deadzone. Scale sets how far one click moves the axis. The default, 256, makes every click one step your robot code can see; smaller values need several clicks before anything changes. At 256 the axis reaches its end after about 128 clicks, around six turns of a typical knob. Pick a larger scale for a knob that should reach the end in fewer turns. Changing the scale zeroes the position. FTC. The FTC Driver Station puts a deadzone on every stick, so in xinput an encoder can’t use a stick axis. It has two other ways out. A trigger count keeps the position. Choose LT or RT under Trigger (xinput) in the knob’s inspector, and the knob counts on that trigger: one step per click, wrapping at 256. The TriggerKnob class turns that back into a running count in your OpMode: java TriggerKnob knob = new TriggerKnob(); // before the loop int clicks = knob.update(gamepad2.left_trigger); // every loop, on the board's gamepad Call update every loop. It stays right as long as the knob turns fewer than 128 clicks between two loops. The count starts at 0 on the first reading, and knob.reset() makes the current position zero. That trigger no longer works as button 15 (LT) or 16 (RT). Each trigger takes one knob, so two knobs can work this way. * Pulsed buttons: one button pulses per click clockwise, another per click anticlockwise, and your OpMode counts the presses. Set them under Direction buttons. If a knob has a trigger, it uses that in xinput and ignores its direction buttons there. Pulsed buttons are available under frc too, if you would rather count clicks than read a position. The shaft push The push switch on each encoder is an ordinary key. Bind it like any other key to a logical button number. Zeroing The board can zero any axis, or all of them, on command — at the start of a match, or when the mechanism it drives is homed.

title: Display tiles and legends
headings: Loading a picture into a slot
Getting them there from a terminal
text: Display tiles and legends A display tile shows text and pictures that can change during a match. On a screen key the display is inside the cap, so the key’s legend changes: the same key can say INTAKE in one part of a match and CLIMB in another. The disp2 colour display shows the same kind of stored pictures on a larger panel, next to the keys rather than in one. The display tiles Tile Panel Keys Pictures disp1 128 × 32 monochrome, 21 columns × 4 rows of text none no, but messages disp2 160 × 128 colour, 13 columns × 8 rows of text none streamed, and 32 stored screenkey1 128 × 128 colour, inside a key cap 1 streamed, and 32 stored disp1 shows readouts: match time, a mechanism state, a message from the robot. disp2 shows the same in colour, plus full-colour pictures: a mode, a target, a status image. screenkey1 is one key whose cap is the screen. All three are ordinary tiles: they go anywhere on the chain and are addressed like any other. Showing text and pictures A display tile shows text in a grid of characters, drawn in the tile’s own font. There are two ways to show a picture: Stream it Store it in a slot Colours Two, dithered Full colour Time to show ~0.2 s, every time A few milliseconds Time to load none a few seconds, once Kept where nowhere; the panel holds it until cleared the tile’s own flash chip Stream a picture you show once. Store the pictures you use as legends. screenkey1 and disp2 each store up to 32 pictures. Each numbered place is a slot. Loading a picture into a slot In the config app’s Configure screen, select the tile (screenkey1 or disp2) and find the Picture section of the inspector. Choose an image file. The app shows you what the tile will actually draw — re-sized and encoded for that panel — not the file you picked. Set send as to a stored picture. Choose the slot and, on a colour panel, the encoding. Full colour is rgb565; the one-bit form is smaller and faster to load. Press Store in slot n. The slot is erased when the transfer starts and holds a picture again only once the whole transfer has arrived and its checksum matches. An interrupted store leaves the slot empty, never half-drawn. If it fails, the app says so; store it again. Checking and reusing stored pictures The Slots section lists the slots, with Show, Load and Erase buttons. Check slots asks the tile what each slot holds: empty, or a picture with its format and size. It takes well under a second. A picture stored from this page is shown by its file name. Load reads a picture back from the tile into the Picture editor. From there you can change its colours or format, or store it in another slot, without the original file. Reading is slower than storing: about 8 seconds for a full-colour picture, 1 second for a two-colour one. Pictures stay on the tile through power cycles. Slot read-back needs current tile firmware; an older tile answers Check slots with an error. Binding legend codes A stored picture is switched by a number, and that number is what robot code sends. A code names an entry in a map, which says which tile and which slot, so the panel layout or the pictures can change without changing robot code. The Legend codes section of the same inspector binds them. There are fifteen codes, 1 to 15, shared by every display tile on the board. Each row picks a slot on the tile you have selected. One code can only point at one tile and slot, so a screenkey1 and a disp2 that change together need a code each. Code Bound to 1 slot 0 — intake.png 2 slot 3 — climb.png 3 unbound A code with no binding does nothing, and so does a binding whose tile is unplugged or whose slot is empty. No error is shown. Zero is never a legend. Zero stops a rumble and leaves every screen unchanged. Bindings are part of your saved configuration, so press Save when you are happy with them. Messages on legend codes A code can also put a prewritten message on any display tile, including a disp1, which cannot store pictures. The message is kept by the main module, so it needs nothing loaded onto the tile. Select the display tile, and write the message in its Rows, with the colours and double height you want. Draw shows it on the panel. Under Messages, pick a code and press Save as code. When the robot sends that code, the panel is cleared and the message is written, so any row you left empty is blank. Load puts a saved message back in the rows to change, and Replace code saves the changes. One code can write a message to several tiles and show a picture on another, so a whole panel can change with one call. On any one tile a code shows either a picture or a message, not both. The main module can hold about 2 KB of messages alongside the rest of your setup: enough for a full four-row message on every code of a disp1. If a message will not fit, the config app says so and keeps your setup as it was. Seeing every code at once The Legends tab lists all fifteen codes and what each one does: the picture it shows, the messages it writes, drawn as the panel shows them, and the key colours it sets. Edit opens the tile that holds that entry. The In the OpMode block at the bottom has the call for every code in use. Getting them there from a terminal Everything above is also a command on the serial channel: python3 tools/bbctl.py --rumble-list # what is bound now python3 tools/bbctl.py --rumble-bind 3 5 0 # code 3 → tile 5, slot 0 Loading a picture is disp <addr> slot <n> begin/data/end, which tools/bb wraps. Next Once the pictures are stored and the codes are bound, the robot can switch between them mid-match — see Changing legends in a match.

title: Changing legends in a match
headings: The number is a legend code, not a key
Changing a key’s colour the same way
There is no way to blank a key
If the board is unplugged mid-match
Do not use it as an animation
text: Changing legends in a match A screen key, a disp2 colour display or a disp1 can show a different legend as the match goes on — INTAKE while you are collecting, SCORE while you are lined up, CLIMB in the endgame. A legend is a stored picture or a prewritten message. This page is how the robot tells the board which one to show. This is the only part of the board that needs code on the robot. It has not yet been confirmed that the FTC Driver Station forwards a rumble call to this board. Test it with your Driver Station before relying on it in a match. How it works In FTC mode the board is an Xbox-style gamepad with no config channel, so during a match the only way to reach it is a gamepad rumble command. The rumble carries a number, and that number selects a stored picture or a prewritten message. Load the legends before the match; switch them during it with one call. The number is a legend code, not a key showLegend(3) does not mean “key 3”. It means “whatever the config app has bound to code 3” — see Binding legend codes. Name the codes in your OpMode for what they mean: static final int LEGEND_INTAKE = 1; static final int LEGEND_SCORE = 2; static final int LEGEND_CLIMB = 3; The panel can then be rearranged — a different key, a different picture — without changing the robot code. Adding the library Copy the files into your project; there is no dependency to add beyond the SDK. From the repository: cp -r robot/ftc/src/org TeamCode/src/main/java/ cp -r robot/ftc/src-ftc/org TeamCode/src/main/java/ That leaves three files in org/firstinspires/ftc/teamcode/buttonboard/. Do not copy test/ — it is for a desktop JDK and Android Studio will try to build it. If your team uses a different package root, change the package line in all three files to match. Requires FTC SDK v7.0 or newer. A minimal OpMode @TeleOp(name = "Button Board legends") public class LegendDemo extends LinearOpMode { static final int LEGEND_INTAKE = 1; static final int LEGEND_SCORE = 2; static final int LEGEND_CLIMB = 3; @Override public void runOpMode() { // gamepad1 must be the pad the Button Board bound as. ButtonBoard board = new ButtonBoard(new GamepadRumbleSink(gamepad1)); waitForStart(); while (opModeIsActive()) { // Safe to call every loop: it sends only when the code changes. if (gamepad1.right_trigger > 0.5) { board.showLegend(LEGEND_CLIMB); } else if (gamepad1.a) { board.showLegend(LEGEND_SCORE); } else { board.showLegend(LEGEND_INTAKE); } telemetry.addData("legend", board.lastLegend()); telemetry.update(); } } } The config app writes this call out for you: the Legends tab has an In the OpMode block with the exact line for every code in use, and a Copy button. The API Call Does showLegend(int code) Show the legend bound to code — unless it is already the last one sent. Returns whether it sent anything. Throws on anything outside 1–15. refresh() Send the last code again regardless. Use it after the board was power-cycled. forget() Drop the remembered code without sending. The next showLegend sends whatever it is given. lastLegend() The last code sent — not what the board is known to be showing. stopRumble() Send zero power. Stops a real gamepad buzzing; does not clear the key. Call it every loop showLegend() suppresses repeats, so call it every loop with the legend that should be showing right now. Use it rather than calling rumble() yourself. Don’t gate legend changes on isRumbling(). It reads true for the length of each step even though the board has no motors, so you would suppress real changes. There is no way to blank a key Zero is the SDK’s stop, so the board ignores it. To show nothing, save an empty message under a code and show that code. If the board is unplugged mid-match Nothing tells you. A board in FTC mode cannot answer. If it is power-cycled it comes back showing whatever its map starts with, while your OpMode still holds the last code it sent — so the next showLegend() of that same code is suppressed and the panel stays wrong. Wire refresh() to a button you can reach. Do not use it as an animation The SDK sends one rumble about every 50 ms and drops any earlier call in that window. The panel always ends on the latest code, but an intermediate one may never appear: flick A → B → C inside 50 ms and B may be skipped. If a legend needs to be seen, leave it up for at least a tenth of a second. Rumble goes to one gamepad. Whichever position the Driver Station gave the board — gamepad1 or gamepad2 — is the one to construct GamepadRumbleSink with. Send to the other and nothing happens, with no error. Changing a key’s colour the same way A code can also recolour keys. In the config app, select a key on an RGB tile, and under Robot colour pick a code, an effect and a colour. When the robot sends that code, the key takes that colour. If the same code also has a legend bound, one showLegend() call changes both, so a key can turn red and read CLIMB at the same moment. This works on a key that is not bound to any button, too. Such a key’s colour belongs to the key itself rather than to a button, which is how you make an indicator light the robot controls. See A key with no button as an indicator light. There are two special colours. ∅ turns the LED off. normal puts the key back on the colour it has in your saved configuration. A code changes only the keys it names. A code followed by another within 50 ms may never arrive, so don’t rely on it. If code 5 means “back to normal”, give code 5 a normal entry for every key your other codes recolour. These colours live on the board’s live LED layer, the same one the Driver Station app writes. They are not saved, and a power cycle or led reset clears them. As with an unplugged board above, call refresh() to put them back. The map holds up to 32 robot colours in total. Setting the board up first Load the pictures, save the messages and bind the codes before you switch to FTC mode. None of it can be done in FTC mode. Put the board in a mode that has the config channel: frc in the config app’s Connect screen. Save, then unplug and plug back in. Load the pictures into slots and bind the codes, and save any messages. Add any robot colours. Check the Legends tab, then Save. Switch back to xinput, save, unplug and plug back in. Check which gamepad position the Driver Station gives it. Your pictures and bindings are kept when you switch back in step 3. The config app offers a “bind the next code” button that waits for a rumble and binds whichever code arrives. Against a real board it will wait forever, because a board that can receive a rumble has no config channel to report it on. It works against the fake board. Bind by picking the number instead; that works everywhere.

title: Install the library
text: Install the library The Button Board can be driven from a program on the Driver Station laptop — reading robot state from NetworkTables and pushing LED colours and display text back to the panel. bb is the Python library for that. You do not need this to use the board. Buttons work through the Driver Station with nothing installed. This is for making the panel react to the robot. What you need Python 3.9 or newer. pyserial. python3 -m pip install pyserial The library itself lives in tools/bb/ in the repository. Copy that directory next to your script, or put its parent on PYTHONPATH: export PYTHONPATH=/path/to/BBRControlBoard/tools Check it works from bb import Board with Board.open() as board: # finds the COM port by itself print(board.hello()) {'ok': True, 'product': 'Button Board', 'fw': '0.1.0', 'proto': 1, ...} If it cannot find the board, pass the port explicitly — Board.open(port="COM7") on Windows, Board.open(port="/dev/ttyACM0") on Linux. Without a board MockBoard lets you write and test a companion app with no hardware attached: from bb import MockBoard board = MockBoard() board.led(3, "red") print(board.state.leds) # {('btn', 3): 'led 3 FF0000'} One connection at a time Only one program can have the board open. If the config app has it open in a browser tab, your script cannot open it, and the other way round. Close one before starting the other.

title: Your first script
text: Your first script A companion app is a loop: read what the robot is doing, decide what the panel should look like, push it. from bb import Board with Board.open() as board: leds = board.led_layer() while True: arm_fault = read_from_networktables("arm_fault") in_range = read_from_networktables("in_scoring_range") leds.set(3, "red" if arm_fault else "off") leds.set(7, "green" if in_range else "off", fx="breathe") leds.flush() led_layer() or board.led() board.led(3, "red") sends a command every time you call it, whether or not the colour changed. led_layer() stages the writes and flush() sends only what changed. Use it for anything that runs in a loop; use board.led() for one-off changes. leds.set(3, "red") leds.flush() # sends: led 3 FF0000 leds.set(3, "red") leds.flush() # sends nothing Colours A colour can be given as: leds.set(1, "red") # a name leds.set(2, "#0040FF") # hex, with or without the # leds.set(3, (0, 64, 255)) # an (r, g, b) triple leds.set(4, 0x0040FF) # an int leds.set(5, None) # off Named colours include red green blue yellow cyan magenta orange purple pink amber lime teal white off, plus alliance_red and alliance_blue. Effects leds.set(3, "red", "blink") # slow flash leds.set(3, "red", "fast") # fast flash leds.set(3, "red", "breathe") # fade in and out An effect keeps running with no further commands. Clearing up board.led_reset() # back to the colours saved in the configuration board.led_all("off") # everything dark, right now led_all("off") is the panic button: it overrides anything else in progress. When the board goes away If the board is disconnected, every call raises BoardError: from bb import Board, BoardError try: leds.flush() except BoardError as e: print("lost the panel:", e) # reconnect, then leds.forget() so the next flush redraws everything Call forget() after a reconnect or a board reboot, so the next flush() resends everything.

title: Python API summary
text: Python API summary Everything here is a method on Board. Each one sends a command and returns the board’s reply as a dictionary, or raises. Connecting Call What it does Board.open(port=None) Open the board, auto-detecting the port board.close() Close it. Also happens on leaving a with block MockBoard() An in-process board, no hardware Identity and state Call Returns board.hello() Product, firmware version, serial, tile count, USB personality board.tiles() A list, one entry per tile: kind, firmware, state, keys currently down board.tile(addr) One tile’s entry, or None board.stats() Uptime, poll cycle time, fault state, LED power budget LEDs Call What it does board.led(btn, colour, fx=None, press=None) Set a logical button’s colour board.led_tile(addr, index, colour, fx=None) Set one LED by tile and position board.led_all(colour) Every LED on every tile board.led_reset() Back to the saved defaults board.led_layer() A diffing writer — see Your first script colour takes a name, "#RRGGBB", "RRGGBB", an (r, g, b) triple, an int, or None for off. fx is "solid", "blink", "fast" or "breathe". press turns the white press-flash on or off for that button. LedLayer Call What it does layer.set(btn, colour, fx, press) Stage a colour layer.set_tile(addr, index, colour, fx) Stage a colour by tile and position layer.flush() Send what changed; returns how many commands went out layer.all(colour) / layer.reset() Send immediately and reset the diff layer.forget() Force the next flush() to resend everything Bindings Call What it does board.bind(btn, add=False) Wait for a key press and bind it. add=True joins a group board.bind_cancel() Stop waiting board.unbind(btn) Remove every key from a button board.unbind(btn, addr, key) Remove one key from a group board.map_get() / board.map_set(m) The whole configuration as a dictionary board.save() Write it to flash bind() blocks until someone presses a key, up to 30 seconds. Encoders Call What it does board.bind_axis(n) Bind axis 1–4 to the next encoder turned board.unbind_axis(n) Remove it board.enc_zero(n=None) Zero one axis, or all of them Display tiles Call What it does board.screen(addr) A row-diffing writer for a display tile screen.text(row, s) / screen.bar(row, col, width, value) Stage a row screen.flush() Send changed rows and commit them together screen.clear() Blank the panel board.disp_store_image(addr, slot, file) Encode an image for the tile and store it in a slot board.disp_slot_show(addr, slot) Show a stored picture: one frame board.disp_slot_info(addr, slot) What a slot holds: None, or its fmt, attr, len and crc board.disp_slot_read(addr, slot) Read a stored picture back, checked against its CRC; seconds for a colour picture board.rumble_text_bind(code, addr, rows, attrs=None) Make a legend code write rows (up to 8 strings) to a display tile; attrs styles each row, e.g. "black on yellow" board.rumble_texts(code=None) / board.rumble_text_unbind(code, addr=None) List or remove those messages Display tiles differ in size: disp1 is 21 columns × 4 rows, disp2 13 × 8 and screenkey1 10 × 8. Take the geometry from screen.cols / screen.rows, which come from the tile’s own descriptor, rather than hard-coding it. MockBoard() includes display tiles to develop against; MockBoard(display=False) behaves like firmware without display support, which answers unknown. The board itself Call What it does board.usb("frc") / board.usb("xinput") Set the USB personality; takes effect at the next reset board.power_budget(mA) Set the LED power budget board.test("walk", 250) / board.test("off") Report button presses with no tile involved board.reset() / board.reset(factory=True) Reboot, optionally erasing the configuration Events The board reports events such as a tile lost, a fault raised, or a key pressed during binding. def on_tile(ev): print(ev["addr"], ev["state"]) # 3 lost unsubscribe = board.on("tile", on_tile) Names are tile, fault, key, enc, progress and player; "*" receives all of them. Callbacks run on the library’s reader thread. Do not call board methods from inside one: the call blocks until it times out. Put the event on a queue and handle it in your loop. Errors Exception When CommandError The board refused the command. .err is the reason code Timeout No reply in time NotConnected The port is closed or the cable went away NoBoardFound Auto-detection could not identify a board BoardError Base class for all of the above

title: Serial command reference
text: Serial command reference The board’s configuration channel is a plain text serial port. The config app, the Python library or a serial terminal such as PuTTY can drive it. You send one command per line, ending in a newline. The board answers with one JSON object per line. Every command produces exactly one final line, either {"ok":true,...} or {"ok":false,"err":"..."}. The board may send event lines at any time, marked with "ev". One can arrive between a command and its reply. Baud rate is ignored; any setting works. Enter must send a newline, not a carriage return. PuTTY’s default sends CR, which this channel ignores: commands appear to be accepted and nothing happens. Set it to send LF, or use bbctl. The commands Command What it does hello Identify the board: firmware, serial, tile count, USB personality tiles Every tile the board knows about stats Uptime, poll cycle time, fault state, power budget usb frc | usb xinput Set the USB personality, applied at the next reset pixel on | pixel off Flash the main module’s light white on every button press. On by default; save keeps the setting bind <btn> Wait for a key press and bind it to that button bind <btn> add Same, but add to the button’s group instead of replacing bind cancel Stop waiting unbind <btn> Remove every key from a button unbind <btn> <addr> <key> Remove one key from a group bind axis <n> Bind axis 1–4 to the next encoder turned unbind axis <n> Remove it enc zero [<n>] Zero one encoder axis, or all of them map get The whole configuration as JSON map set <json> Replace it save Write configuration to flash and verify it led <btn> <rgb> [fx] [press] Live colour for a logical button led tile <addr> <led> <rgb> [fx] Live colour by tile and LED number led all <rgb> Every LED. led all off is the panic button led reset Discard the live layer; back to saved defaults power budget <mA> Set the LED power budget test walk [ms] Press buttons 1→32 in turn, with no tile involved test hold <btn> Hold one button test all Every button at once test off Stop disp <addr> … Write text, a bar or a picture to a display tile disp <addr> slot <n> … Store, show, erase, check (info) or read back (read) one of the tile’s saved pictures replace <old> <new> Move a tile’s bindings to another address by hand reset Reboot reset factory Erase the configuration and reboot boot Reboot into the USB bootloader for a firmware update rgb is six hex digits or off. fx is solid, blink, fast or breathe. Addresses are 1–31, logical buttons 1–32, keys count from 0. Events Event When tile A tile went online, was lost, was assigned an address, or entered its bootloader fault The fault indicator changed, with the reason key A key was pressed — only while waiting for a binding enc An encoder was turned — only while waiting for a binding progress During a tile firmware update player The FTC Driver Station assigned this board a player number rumble A rumble packet arrived, with the legend code it decodes to — FTC mode only A client that only wants request and response can ignore every line containing "ev". A worked example > hello < {"ok":true,"product":"Button Board","fw":"0.1.0","proto":1,"tiles":3,"mode":"run","usb":"frc"} > bind 7 < {"ev":"key","addr":1,"key":4} < {"ok":true,"btn":7,"addr":1,"key":4,"sources":1} > led 7 FF8800 blink < {"ok":true} > save < {"ok":true,"saved":true} bbctl tools/bbctl.py in the repository is a console for this channel. It sends the right newline endings, holds the port open so test mode survives, and reads past event lines to the reply. python3 tools/bbctl.py # interactive console python3 tools/bbctl.py hello stats # run and exit python3 tools/bbctl.py -p COM7 "test walk 250" # explicit port

title: Troubleshooting
headings: Nothing appears when I plug it in
The config app cannot see the board
A tile is missing from the chain
Buttons stick on, or fire on their own
Is the board sending my presses at all?
The Driver Station sees the wrong thing
LEDs are dimmer than I set them
text: Troubleshooting Nothing appears when I plug it in Try a different USB cable. Charge-only cables are common and carry no data. Check the power LED on the main module. Dark means it is not getting power. Hold the CFG button while plugging in. That forces a known-good USB configuration whatever is stored; use it when a saved configuration has made the board unreachable. If it still does nothing, hold BOOTSEL while plugging in. An RPI-RP2 drive appearing means the hardware is alive and the firmware is the problem — see Updating the firmware. The config app cannot see the board Are you in Chrome or Edge? The app does not work in Firefox or Safari. Is something else holding the port? A serial terminal, another browser tab, or a running Python script will each keep the port to itself. Close it. You must pick the port from the browser’s dialog. The page cannot open one on its own. A tile is missing from the chain Check these, most likely first: A cable not fully clicked home. A damaged cable. Swap it with a known-good one. Check Diagnose → Counters. A tile accumulating checksum errors or missed replies is a wiring problem. A tile that never appears at all is more likely a cable or a dead board. A key does nothing Is it bound? An unbound key registers nowhere. Check Configure. Does the tile see it at all? Diagnose shows presses straight off the bus, before binding. If it shows there and not in the Driver Station, the problem is the binding or the Driver Station. If it does not show there, it is the switch. Hot-swap sockets: pull the switch and look at the pins. A bent pin folds under the switch instead of entering the socket. Buttons stick on, or fire on their own A worn microswitch chattering — raise that tile’s debounce. If every button on a tile misbehaves at once, suspect the bus rather than the switches: check the counters and the cable. Is the board sending my presses at all? The main module’s small RGB light flashes white each time the board sends a button press over USB, in every personality including xinput. Flashes, but the Driver Station sees nothing: the board is fine. Check the personality and the Driver Station’s own settings. No flash: the key is not bound, the tile is lost, or the board is in bind mode. Check Configure. Never flashes at all: it may be turned off. It is the Status light checkbox on the Connect screen. The Driver Station sees the wrong thing FRC expects frc; FTC expects xinput. Check on the Connect screen. A personality change only takes effect at a USB reset. Unplug and plug back in. Under FTC, bind the pad with Start+A or Start+B as usual. A key bound as a Start+A or Start+B combo does it in one press (see Binding buttons). Use Diagnose → Test to settle where the problem is: it makes the board report presses with no tile involved. If the Driver Station sees those, everything from the board to the laptop is fine and the problem is on the bus or in the bindings. LEDs are dimmer than I set them The power budget is limiting them. The board lowers global brightness until the panel fits the current it can draw from USB. Diagnose → Power shows the budget, the worst case and the brightness in use. Raise the budget if the port genuinely supplies more. If the panel cannot fit even at minimum brightness, the LEDs are held off and a fault is raised — the same view says so. My configuration disappeared It was probably never saved. Changes work immediately but live in RAM until Save is pressed. Unplugging before that discards them. Everything worked yesterday Check firmware versions on Connect and Diagnose. A tile updated to firmware the main module does not understand is reported as incompatible and is not used.
